newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania in new election crisis.
newsitem.headline: Albania in new election crisis.

text.p: The chaotic Balkan state of Albania was set for further turmoil on Wednesday over elections called to stop its slide to violence but which most parties in a national unity government may boycott.
President Sali Berisha was expected to name the day for new elections, due at the end of June, although a boycott by other parties would turn them into a mockery.

The early elections are part of efforts to stop the orgy of rioting that erupted in Albania in February and March after the collapse of pyramid investment schemes and are seen as vital to prevent a return to violence.

The elections became mired in dispute after Berisha's Democratic Party forced an election law through parliament which the other parties in the Government of National Reconciliation said favoured Berisha.
The law was also seen as a snub to the Organisation for Security and Cooperation and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), which had brokered the talks and was seeking a law backed by all parties.
Although Albania is far calmer now, sporadic violence and killings are still common and volleys of gunfire echo through the night in the capital. A curfew is still in place throughout the country.
The election law was a key element of the six-point political contract brokered by European envoy Franz Vranitzky and signed by the Democrats and the eight other government parties.
The eight, spearheaded by the second-largest party in parliament, the Socialists, threatened to boycott the elections if the law was passed.
The pro-Berisha newspaper Albania said the president would call the elections for June 29 and that parliament would be dissolved today.
The Socialist newspaper Zeri I Poppulit said Berisha had "swindled" the nation while leading independent newspaper Kohe Jone said Berisha was playing "cat and mouse".
"Sali Berisha, a president elected by an unelected parliament, is a person who has never been ready to change, never been ready to accept negotiations and free elections," the newspaper said.
It was not known whether the parties would carry out their threat to boycott the vote. Socialist Party leader Fatos Nano was planning a news conference at 1100/0900 GMT.
Prime Minister Bashkim Fino, also a Socialist, has been in Washington while the domestic crisis brewed but was expected back in the country in the early afternoon.
The Socialists boycotted the last elections in May 1996, which gave the Democrats an overwhelming majority in parliament but which was called flawed by international observers.
Berisha was to travel to the town of Kavaja, some 50 kms (30 miles) from Tirana, a stronghold of support, where he was expected to kick off his election campaign.
The OSCE was said to be disappointed by the Democratic Party's forcing through of its own law and said it would wait and see what the other parties decided.
"They are pondering their position, things are very much up in the air," one Western diplomat said.

Another key point of the Vranitzky contract was the disbanding of so-called salvation committees, formed mostly in the south of the country at the time of the rioting to bring back order as the state administration collapsed.
They have said they will only disband if the elections are guaranteed to be free and fair.
A meeting of the committees is due on May 16, where they will discuss whether to disband or not.
